combining: First give each criterion a band: Low, Medium or High. Then start from the band that most criteria share. Mostly Low points to a rating of 1 or 2, mostly Medium to 3 to 5 and mostly High to 6 or 7. The other bands then move you up or down. All Medium is about 4; mostly Medium with one Low is about 3; mostly Medium with one High is about 5. These are rules of thumb, not a formula.
example: Take a study of whether a brain-training app improves memory. The title, 'Brain-training app may boost memory', leaves out how small the test was (Medium). Readers need a university login to see the full paper (Medium). It appeared in a peer-reviewed journal that accepts most papers it receives (Medium). It builds on memory research but assumes that better scores in the app mean a better memory in daily life (Medium). 30 volunteers took part, with no comparison group and no shared data (Low). The authors say the app may help but do not mention that people improve at any test with practice (Medium). That is mostly Medium with one Low, so about 3 is a fair rating.
accessNote: Access is about openness. It asks who can read the full study and whether they must pay, log in or ask for a copy. It does not tell you whether the findings are correct. A free paper can be poor and a paywalled one excellent. So rate Access on openness alone and judge the evidence with the other five criteria.
